summary: Describes extensions to Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for use in multipoint and multicast networks, where one sender serves many receivers. It updates RFC 5880 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8562 extends Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) for multipoint and multicast paths. One head sends regular checks, and each tail detects a failure if the checks stop arriving.

questions: what is a bfd multipoint head and tail
how does a bfd tail detect failure
subtitle: Use one-way BFD control packets so many receivers can detect loss of a multipoint path.

tldr.problem: Traditional BFD checks connectivity between two systems, but a multipoint path has one sender and many receivers and may have no return path.
tldr.mechanism: A head periodically sends BFD Control packets marked as multipoint. Each tail declares failure when packets stop arriving before its Detection Time.
tldr.outcome: Tails can detect a failed path without sending BFD packets back. RFC 8562 updates RFC 5880 and is updated by RFC 9780.

facts.label: Detection Time
facts.value: Desired Min TX Interval multiplied by Detect Mult

today: RFC 8562 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2019. It updates RFC 5880, and the unit metadata says RFC 9780 updates it.

sections.title: BFD for One Sender and Many Receivers
sections.content:
Base BFD verifies unicast connectivity between a pair of systems. This extension verifies one-way connectivity from a multipoint sender, called the head, to one or more receivers, called tails.

A tail can monitor the path even when it has no return path to the head. If a return path exists, a separate extension described in RFC 8563 can let a tail notify the head. Most timing and options are controlled by the head.
sections.plainLanguage: The head sends BFD checks to all tails on a multipoint path. Each tail can detect that the path stopped working without sending a reply.

sections.title: How a Tail Detects Failure
sections.content:
The head periodically sends BFD Control packets down the multipoint path. Each packet gives tails the timer information needed to calculate a Detection Time.

If a tail receives no BFD Control packet before its Detection Time expires, it declares the path failed. This mechanism does not tell the head whether each tail can still receive packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tail calculates how long it can wait without a BFD packet. If that time passes with no packet, the tail reports the path as failed.

sections.title: The Head and Tail Session Types
sections.content:
A MultipointHead session sends BFD Control packets over one multipoint path and receives none. A MultipointTail session receives packets from the head on that path. The ordinary PointToPoint session remains available alongside them.

The head session is administratively controlled and does not fail through packet loss. A tail session fails when it loses contact with the head or the head is administratively disabled. A failed tail may notify the user through another mechanism, such as logging or NETCONF.
sections.plainLanguage: The head session sends checks, while each tail session listens for them. A head does not learn tail status from BFD unless another reporting mechanism is used.

sections.title: Tail State and Session Setup
sections.content:
There is no three-way setup handshake because many tails receive packets from one head. MultipointHead sessions MUST NOT send the INIT state, and a receiver MUST ignore such packets.

A tail changes from Down to Up when it receives a packet reporting Up. It returns to Down when it receives Down or AdminDown, or when its Detection Timer expires. A head has no Detection Timer; its state changes are controlled administratively.
sections.plainLanguage: A tail moves to Up after receiving an Up packet from the head. It returns to Down when the head reports a down state or its timer expires.

sections.title: Finding Sessions and Calculating Timers
sections.content:
The head sets its My Discriminator to a value bound to the multipoint path and sets Your Discriminator to zero. A tail identifies a session using the source address, My Discriminator, and path identity. The head's discriminator MUST NOT change during the session.

A tail's Detection Time is the last received Desired Min TX Interval multiplied by Detect Mult. For IP multicast, a tail identifies BFD by destination UDP port 3784. The head SHOULD send packets with the P bit when timer values change and must continue using the old interval while raising its transmit interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The tail uses the packet source and path information to identify which head it is hearing. Its timeout depends on the interval advertised by the head and the detection multiplier.

sections.title: Packet Checks and Transmission Rules
sections.content:
Receivers discard packets with invalid fields, including a version other than 1, a zero Detect Mult, or a zero My Discriminator. The minimum Length is 24 when the authentication bit is clear, or 26 when it is set. A multipoint packet with a nonzero Your Discriminator is discarded.

Periodic transmissions MUST be jittered by reducing the interval by a random value from 0 to 25%. A MultipointTail MUST NOT transmit BFD Control packets. On an IP multicast group, a tail MUST consume BFD packets rather than forward them to receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers discard malformed packets and consume valid BFD packets on the multicast path. The head varies its send interval slightly to reduce synchronization with other systems.

sections.title: Congestion and Authentication Risks
sections.content:
For BFD over multiple hops, an implementation MUST have congestion control and MUST reduce its traffic when congestion is detected. The mechanism for controlling BFD load is outside this document.

Implementations that create tail sessions dynamically need limits to prevent an unlimited number of sessions. Shared authentication keys let one tail impersonate the head to other tails, so shared keys are a security exposure unless all tails are trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD traffic must decrease when a multipoint network is congested. Dynamic tail sessions also need limits, and a shared key is risky when tails cannot all be trusted.

transitions.label: Receive DOWN or ADMIN DOWN, or timer expires
